title: Biogeochemical Cycles and Ecological Succession

cards.b:
Plants and animals use the same atoms again and again. These loops are the biogeochemical cycles. UPSC asks about them in Prelims, and they explain pollution problems such as eutrophication, acid rain and fertiliser overuse.

Succession explains how bare land turns into forest and why a disturbed ecosystem recovers. Both topics are short, but they carry sure marks.

In a gaseous cycle the main reservoir is the atmosphere or ocean. Carbon, nitrogen and oxygen cycles are gaseous. In a sedimentary cycle the reservoir is the Earth’s crust. Phosphorus and sulphur are sedimentary (sulphur has a small gas phase).

Cycles move through pools (reservoirs) and fluxes (flows). Humans now change the flows more than nature does.

Plants take in CO2 by photosynthesis. Respiration, decomposition and burning return it. The biggest store is the rocks (limestone and fossil fuels). Among active stores, the ocean is the largest.

Burning fossil fuels moves ancient carbon into the air in a few centuries. That is why CO2 has gone past 420 ppm (as of 2025) from about 280 ppm before industry.

cards.h: Why free nitrogen is useless to plants
cards.b:
Air is about 78 percent nitrogen, but plants cannot use it directly. Nitrogen fixation converts it. Bacteria such as Rhizobium (in legume roots), Azotobacter and cyanobacteria like Nostoc do this. Lightning also fixes some.

Then ammonification makes ammonia from dead matter. Nitrification turns it into nitrite (Nitrosomonas) and nitrate (Nitrobacter). Denitrification (Pseudomonas) returns nitrogen gas to air.

Phosphorus comes from rock weathering. It has no gas phase. It is often the limiting nutrient in fresh water. Excess phosphate from detergents and fertiliser causes eutrophication: algal bloom, oxygen loss, fish kills.

Sulphur enters the air as SO2 from volcanoes and burning coal. It becomes sulphuric acid in acid rain. Plankton also release dimethyl sulphide, which helps form clouds.

Succession is the orderly change of a community over time. Primary succession starts on bare ground with no soil: new lava, rock or a retreating glacier. Pioneers such as lichens come first (a lithosere). On open water it is a hydrosere.

Secondary succession starts where soil survives: after a fire, flood or abandoned farm. It is much faster.

The steps are called seral stages. The final stable community is the climax community. Early on, production exceeds respiration; at climax they roughly balance.

Autogenic succession is driven by the community itself. Allogenic succession is driven by outside forces such as climate. Species diversity and soil depth rise with time.

Clements (early 20th century) argued for a single climate climax in a region (monoclimax). Later ecologists such as Gleason and Tansley stressed that local soil and chance matter, so many end states are possible.

Modern thinking sees ecosystems as shifting, not fixed. This matters for restoration policy: you cannot simply plant any tree and expect the old forest.

Over-use of urea has unbalanced India’s nitrogen cycle. The government pushed neem-coated urea (2015), the Soil Health Card (2015) and nano urea to cut waste. Run-off nitrate and phosphate cause algal blooms in lakes.

Secondary succession is the basis of natural regeneration in jhum fallows of the North-East and in mine land reclamation. Mangrove colonisation in the Sundarbans is a classic example of succession in a delta.

Mains-style: “Discuss the impact of excessive fertiliser use on the nitrogen and phosphorus cycles in India.” Structure: explain both cycles briefly; show the imbalance (eutrophication, groundwater nitrate, N2O emissions); give policy (neem-coated urea, nano urea, soil health card, organic farming).

Mains-style: “Distinguish primary and secondary succession with examples.”

Prelims tip: Phosphorus has no gaseous phase. Denitrification returns N2 to air. Succession on rock is a lithosere; on water, a hydrosere.

quiz.q: Which cycle has no significant gaseous phase?
quiz.w: Phosphorus moves through rocks, soil and water only.

quiz.q: Bacteria that fix nitrogen in legume roots belong to:
quiz.w: Rhizobium forms root nodules. Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter nitrify. Pseudomonas denitrifies.

quiz.q: Conversion of nitrate back to nitrogen gas is:
quiz.w: Denitrification, done by bacteria like Pseudomonas, returns N2 to the air.

quiz.q: The largest store of carbon on Earth is:
quiz.w: Carbonate rocks and fossil fuels hold far more carbon than the air or biosphere.

quiz.q: Succession on a newly formed bare rock is called:
quiz.w: No soil exists, so it is primary. Lichens are typical pioneers.
Soil and seeds already exist after a fire or flood, so recovery is faster.

quiz.q: Eutrophication is mainly triggered by excess:
quiz.w: Nutrients feed algal blooms that deplete oxygen.

quiz.q: Succession in a pond leading to land is a:
quiz.w: A hydrosere starts in water. A lithosere starts on rock.
Nitrosomonas makes nitrite; Nitrobacter makes nitrate.

quiz.q: The final stable stage of succession is the:
quiz.w: The climax community is relatively stable under existing conditions.
